What is JWT and what are its three parts?

A JWT is a compact, URL-safe token: Header (alg, typ) . Payload (claims) . Signature. The server verifies the signature, so it can trust the claims without a DB or session lookup. That's what makes it stateless.
Is JWT encrypted? Where is it stored?

A signed JWT (JWS) is only Base64URL-encoded, so anyone can read it. Don't put secrets in it. Use JWE if you need encryption. Storage: an HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie protects against XSS (add CSRF protection). Memory or localStorage is simpler but exposed to XSS. A common pattern is the access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.
Registered claims?

iss (issuer), sub (subject or user id), aud (audience), exp (expiry), nbf (not before), iat (issued at), jti (unique token id, used for revocation lists). You can add custom claims such as roles or tenant.
How do you log out / revoke a JWT?

JWTs can't be "deleted", because they're valid until exp. Options: short expiry plus refresh tokens, a denylist of jti values in Redis until expiry, a per-user token version or "password changed at" claim, and rotating and revoking refresh tokens in the DB.
Session-based vs token-based authentication?

Session | JWT
Server stores the session; the client holds a JSESSIONID cookie | Server stores nothing; the token carries the state
Easy to revoke | Hard to revoke
Scaling needs sticky sessions or a shared store (Redis) | Scales horizontally; good for microservices and mobile
HS256 vs RS256?

HS256 is symmetric: the same secret signs and verifies, so every verifier has to know the secret. RS256 is asymmetric: the auth server signs with a private key, and services verify with the public key published at a JWKS endpoint. Prefer RS256 in microservices.
Common JWT security mistakes?

Accepting alg: none · weak secrets · not checking exp/aud/iss · long-lived access tokens · putting PII in the payload · sending tokens over plain HTTP · storing them in localStorage without XSS protection.
Why are JWTs Base64URL and not plain Base64?

Standard Base64 uses +, / and =, which have meanings in URLs and need escaping. Base64URL uses - and _, and removes padding, so a token can go in a URL, form or header unchanged. Encoding is reversible, and gives no confidentiality.
Can you change the payload of a JWT? What happens?

Anyone can decode, edit and re-encode it. But the signature covers the original bytes, so verification fails without the key. Even changing whitespace in the JSON invalidates it. So a JWT is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof, and it is secret only if encrypted.
JWS vs JWE: when would you use encryption?

JWS provides integrity; JWE provides confidentiality. Use JWE, or better, an opaque token, if claims must be hidden from the client or from intermediaries. A token can be nested: signed, then encrypted. JWE adds cost and complexity, so first ask whether that data needs to be in the token.
Which signing algorithm would you choose today, and why?

For one app that issues and verifies, HS256 with a strong random secret is adequate. For several services or third parties, use asymmetric: RS256 for compatibility, ES256 or EdDSA for smaller tokens, in a stack that supports them. The choice is about key distribution, more than about speed.
Is RS256 slower? Does it matter?

RSA signing is slow, on the order of milliseconds; RSA verification is fast, because the public exponent is small. HMAC is the fastest in both directions. ECDSA signing is fast, and its verifying is slower than RSA's. Tokens are signed rarely and verified often, so RS256 suits that pattern. In practice, for a typical API, this cost is small compared with I/O.
How does a resource server know which public key to use?

The token's header has a kid, and the server fetches the issuer's JWKS, usually found through OIDC discovery. It caches keys, and refreshes on an unknown kid. The JWKS URL must come from your configuration, not from the token.
Explain the algorithm confusion attack in detail.

The server signs with RS256. An attacker takes the public key, sets alg to HS256, and computes an HMAC using the bytes of that public key as the secret. A flawed verifier reads alg, and calls HMAC with its "verification key", which is that same public key, so the signature matches. The attacker can now forge any token. The fix is to pin the algorithm to the key, as modern libraries do with typed keys.
Why is the aud claim important?

All services trusting one issuer accept its signature. Without an audience check, a token for a weak service, even for a compromised one, is accepted by the payments service. The check binds a token to its intended recipient. Spring's resource server does not validate it unless you set audiences.
Why not just make the JWT long-lived?

A JWT cannot be recalled without extra state. A 30-day token that leaks is a 30-day breach, and its claims go stale, such as roles after a demotion. Short-lived access tokens with server-tracked refresh tokens keep the fast path stateless while preserving control.
Why make the refresh token opaque rather than a JWT?

A refresh token is checked against the database anyway, for revocation and rotation, so a self-contained format adds nothing. An opaque random value reveals no data, cannot be mistaken for an access token, and is simple. Store only its hash.
Explain refresh token rotation. What attack does it address?

Each refresh returns a new token and marks the old one used. It limits the value of a stolen token. If an old token reappears, both parties have the same chain, so the server revokes the family, forcing login. It addresses long-term undetected token theft, especially in public clients without a client secret.
In a rotation implementation, revokeFamily runs and then an exception is thrown. What can go wrong?

With a plain @Transactional, the runtime exception rolls back the transaction, undoing the revocation. The attacker's family stays valid. Use noRollbackFor, return a result rather than throwing, or do the revocation in a REQUIRES_NEW method on another bean.
Two browser tabs refresh at the same moment and the user is logged out. Why, and how do you fix it?

Both tabs send the same refresh cookie. The first rotates it; the second looks like reuse. Fix on the client with one shared in-flight refresh, or a cross-tab lock such as the Web Locks API. On the server, allow a short grace window, and lock the row. Log these so that you can distinguish them from real attacks.
How do you log out a user everywhere?

Revoke all the user's refresh token families. For access tokens, bump a tokenVersion on the user, or store a cutoff time, and reject older tokens; this needs a cached per-request lookup. If you accept up to 15 minutes of delay, revoking refresh tokens alone is enough.
How would you implement a jti denylist efficiently?

On logout, write SET denylist:{jti} 1 EX {remaining seconds} to Redis. The filter checks EXISTS after verifying the signature, not before, so that attackers cannot cause lookups cheaply. The TTL frees entries automatically. For scale, a Bloom filter or local cache can avoid some lookups. If Redis is down, you must decide whether to fail open or closed; for high-value APIs, fail closed.
localStorage or cookie for tokens?

There is no universally right answer; each has a risk. localStorage is exposed to XSS, with persistent theft. Cookies are exposed to CSRF, which is well understood and can be mitigated with SameSite and tokens. So: access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, or use a BFF with no tokens in the browser. State that XSS still lets an attacker act on the page.
Does putting a JWT in a cookie bring back CSRF?

Yes. CSRF depends on automatic sending, and cookies are sent automatically, whatever they hold. Use SameSite, plus an anti-CSRF token or custom header. Bearer-in-header JWTs are immune only because JavaScript must attach them explicitly.
Output: what does the first segment of eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.xxx. decode to, and what should a server do?

The first part decodes to {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}, which was checked with Node. That header indicates an unsigned token. A correct server rejects it, even if the payload looks fine and the third segment is empty. JJWT's parseSignedClaims throws, since there is no signature.
Why does an expired token produce a 500 in many hand-written filters?

JJWT throws ExpiredJwtException from the filter. Filters run outside DispatcherServlet, so @ControllerAdvice never sees it, and it is not an AuthenticationException, so ExceptionTranslationFilter rethrows it. The result is a 500. Catch JwtException in the filter and call the entry point.
Should the JWT filter load the user from the database on each request?

The trade-off is freshness against statelessness. Claims only: fast, no lookup, stale for up to the TTL. Loading the user: detects disabled accounts immediately, but adds a query to each request, and removes the main benefit. A middle path uses claims, with a small cached check for high-risk operations.
Clock differences between servers cause random 401s. What do you do?
Run NTP on all hosts, and allow a small leeway, as with clockSkewSeconds(30); Spring's default skew is 60 seconds. A large leeway extends the token's real lifetime, so keep it small.
Session cookie vs JWT for a typical company web application?

For one server-rendered or same-site app, a session is simpler and easier to revoke. Stateless JWTs help where tokens cross domains or services, for mobile clients, or with a separate identity provider. "JWT because it scales" is weak: Spring Session with Redis scales well, too. A stateful session is often right, and the question is about revocation and topology.
How would you make a stolen access token useless?

Bind it to the client: DPoP (RFC 9449) has the client sign each request with a private key, with the public key's thumbprint in the token. mTLS (RFC 8705) binds it to a client certificate. A thief with only the token cannot produce the proof. Without these, a bearer token is usable by whoever holds it.
What is the difference between JWT and PASETO?

PASETO is an alternative token format that fixes the algorithm by version, so there is no alg header to attack. It removes the classic confusion and none bugs, by design. JWT is the established standard, and needed for OIDC interoperability, and those bugs are solved by correct libraries.
Design: authentication for a web app, a mobile app, and 10 microservices.

- Use an identity provider with OIDC, Authorization Code + PKCE for both clients.
- Web: BFF with a cookie session. Mobile: refresh tokens in the Keychain or Keystore, with rotation.
- Access tokens: JWT, 5 to 15 minutes, ES256 or RS256, with aud per API, and keys from JWKS.
- A gateway validates and rate-limits; each service validates again.
- Service-to-service uses client credentials or token exchange.
- Logout revokes refresh tokens; critical operations re-check state in the database.
How do you authenticate a WebSocket connection with a JWT?

The browser WebSocket API cannot send an Authorization header. With STOMP, send Authorization: Bearer ... in the CONNECT frame headers. In a ChannelInterceptor on the inbound channel, decode it with the JwtDecoder and call accessor.setUser(...). Then message-level security (@EnableWebSocketSecurity) can authorize destinations. Alternatives are a same-site cookie with an Origin check on the handshake, or a short-lived one-time ticket in the URL. Handle token expiry on long-lived connections.
Opaque access tokens vs JWT access tokens?

JWT: verified locally with a cached public key, so it is fast and needs no network call. But it is hard to revoke before exp, and its claims are readable by anyone who holds it. Opaque: revocation is immediate, and nothing leaks. But every check is an introspection call, which adds latency and makes the authorization server a dependency on the request path. Big platforms often use both: opaque outside and JWT inside (the phantom token pattern).
Should the Angular app send the ID token or the access token to the API?

Always the access token. The ID token's audience is the client app. It is meant for the client to learn who logged in, and it carries no API scopes. An API that accepts ID tokens can be fed a token issued to any client of the same identity provider. The resource server must check that aud is the API. 💡 With the BFF pattern, the browser holds neither token, only a session cookie.
An admin removes a user's ADMIN role, but the user's JWT still says ADMIN. What do you do?

The token is a snapshot of the user's rights. The options are:
- Short access-token lifetimes (5 to 15 minutes), so the change applies at the next refresh. Make the refresh endpoint re-read the roles from the database.
- A token version or "roles changed at" value per user. Compare it with the token's iat in a cheap cached check, and reject older tokens.
- Revoke the user's refresh tokens and add the current jti to a denylist.
- For highly sensitive operations, check permissions in the database rather than trusting claims.
Why should a JWT never be put in a URL query parameter?

URLs are recorded in many places: web server and proxy access logs, browser history, bookmarks, analytics, and the Referer header sent to other sites. Anyone with access to those can replay the token until it expires. Use the Authorization header or a secure cookie. If a URL is unavoidable (a download link or WebSocket handshake), use a dedicated, short-lived, single-use, narrowly scoped ticket, not the access token.
In a microservice chain, should every service validate the JWT, or only the gateway?

Every service should validate it (zero trust). Local verification with cached JWKS keys costs microseconds. Trusting a header like X-User-Id from "inside the network" means any compromised pod, or a request that bypasses the gateway, can impersonate any user. The gateway handles coarse checks such as authentication, rate limits and routing. Each service checks iss, aud, exp and its own fine-grained authorization. For calls between services, forward the user token or exchange it for a down-scoped token. Do not invent your own headers.
Hand-written JWT filter vs oauth2ResourceServer().jwt(): which should you build?

| Custom OncePerRequestFilter | Resource server support
Who issues tokens | Usually your own login endpoint | An authorization server (Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta)
Validation code | You write and test it | Built in: signature, exp, nbf, iss
Key rotation | Manual | Keys fetched from JWKS by kid
Error responses | Easy to get wrong (500 on expired token) | 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header
Customizing roles | Your code | JwtAuthenticationConverter
Rule of thumb: if an identity provider issues the tokens, use the resource server; it is a few lines of config. A custom filter makes sense only when your app issues its own tokens, and even then you can configure the resource server with your own key.
issuer-uri vs jwk-set-uri vs public-key-location: how should the resource server get its key?

| issuer-uri | jwk-set-uri | public-key-location
Where keys come from | Discovered from the issuer's metadata | The JWKS URL you give | A PEM file you ship
Validates iss | Yes | Only if issuer-uri is also set | Not by itself
Key rotation | Automatic | Automatic | Redeploy with the new key
Needs the IdP reachable | Yes, for metadata and keys | Yes, for keys | No
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://sso.example.com/realms/ehr
Rule of thumb: start with issuer-uri. Add jwk-set-uri when the metadata endpoint is not reachable from the service, for example a different internal host. Use a static key only for your own tokens or offline tests.
JWT vs API key vs mTLS for service-to-service calls?

| JWT (client credentials) | API key | mTLS
Proves | Caller identity, scopes, expiry | Possession of a shared secret | Possession of a private key, at the connection
Expires | Minutes | Until rotated by hand | When the certificate expires
Carries permissions | Yes, in claims | Looked up on the server | Only identity, from the certificate
Operational cost | Authorization server | Low | Certificate issuing and rotation, often a service mesh
Leaked credential | Useful until exp | Useful until revoked | Key must be stolen, not just a header
Rule of thumb: client-credentials JWTs are the usual choice inside a platform that already has an authorization server. API keys suit simple external integrations. mTLS secures the channel and pairs well with JWTs rather than replacing them.
JJWT vs Nimbus JOSE + JWT vs Auth0 java-jwt: which library?

| JJWT | Nimbus JOSE + JWT | Auth0 java-jwt
Style | Fluent builder, small API | Full JOSE toolkit | Simple builder and verifier
JWE (encryption) | Yes (since 0.12) | Yes | No
JWKS handling | Basic | Rich (remote key sets, caching) | Via separate jwks-rsa library
Used by Spring Security | No | Yes, inside NimbusJwtDecoder | No
Rule of thumb: in a Spring app, you rarely need a separate library: the resource server already uses Nimbus, and NimbusJwtEncoder can issue tokens. JJWT is common in tutorials with custom filters; know that its 0.11 and 0.12 APIs differ.
